Fazal Rahman son of Dost Muhammad
Present:- M/S Hafiz Ashfaq Ahmad, ASC & Akhtar Saeed,
Mr. Imran Khan, Astt: A.G, for State.
Mr. Shah Irani, AHC, for respondents/complainant-
party i.e. legal heirs of both the deceased.
body: SALAH-UD-DIN, J.- The appellant, namely Fazal Rahman, has called in question the judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 16.09.2025, passed by the learned Sessions Judge/ Zilla Qazi, Shangla, in case FIR No. 412 dated 07.10.2024, registered U/Ss 302, 200 and 201 PPC, R/W section 15-AA, at Police Station Alpuri, District Shangla. Vide the impugned judgment, rendered upon conclusion of a full-fledged trial in Sessions Case No. 72/2 of 2024, the appellant was convicted and sentenced as under:- Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din “ 32. In view of the above, I hold that the prosecution successfully proved the charge u/s 302 (b) PPC against the accused facing trial beyond any shadow of reasonable doubt of committing the brutal murder of his mother Mst. Rabia Bibi and wife Mst. Gul Badan in a most heinous and revolting manner.

Accordingly accused facing trial Fazal Rahman S/O Dost Muhammad Khan R/O Kog Basi, Tehsil Alpurai District Shangla is convicted u/s 302 (b) PPC and sentenced to Death (on two counts) as tazir i.e. one each for murder of his mother Mst. Rabia Bibi and wife Mst. Gul Badan. He shall also pay compensation of Rs, 30,00,000/- (three million) to the legal heirs of each deceased as required u/s 544-A, Cr.P.C. In case of default in payment, the amount, shall be recovered as an arrears of land revenue. The sentence of death shall be executed by hanging the convict by the neck till he is dead, subject to confirmation by the Hon'ble Peshawar High court u/s 374 Cr.P.C.
34. The Benefit of section 382-B Cr.P.C is extended to the convict, allowing the period already spent in custody to be counted towards his substantive sentence, except for the death penalty.

33. Further the accused is also convicted u/s 15- AA and sentenced to three (03) years RI along with fine of Rs. 3000/- In case of default of payment, he shall undergo simple imprisonment for one-month.

35. As far as the offence under sections 200/201 PPC is concerned, the same has not been proved by the prosecution through cogent evidence. Therefore, the accused facing trial is acquitted u/s 200/201 PPC.”
2. Arguments of learned counsel for parties, as well as learned Astt: A.G for State were heard and requestioned record gone through with their valuable assistance.

3. According to the prosecution case, the complainant, Aman Ullah, reported the matter to the local police at DHQ Hospital, Alpuri, stating therein Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din that one of the deceased, namely Mst. Rabia Bibi, was his mother, whereas the other deceased, namely Mst. Gul Badan, was his sister-in-law (بھابی), who had been married to his stepbrother, Fazal Rahman (the appellant herein), about 15/16 years prior to the occurrence. Out of the said wedlock, the couple had a daughter aged about 14/15 years. Owing to strained matrimonial relations, Mst. Gul Badan had left her matrimonial home and gone to her parental home 2/3 days prior to the occurrence. On the day of occurrence, at the direction of his mother (Mst. Rabia Bibi), the complainant visited the house of his sister-in-law; however, she was unwilling to return to her matrimonial home. At about 14:00 hours, the complainant was present with his mother, Mst. Rabia Bibi, in a residential room of their house. In the meanwhile, the appellant, armed with a pistol, arrived there and opened fire upon his stepmother, who sustained a firearm injury and, in an injured condition, ran towards a nearby bathroom to seek shelter. The appellant, however, pursued her and again opened fire upon her inside the bathroom. The complainant, owing to sheer fear, could neither resist Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din nor intervene. After the appellant's departure, the complainant found his mother lying in the bathroom, smeared in blood. Upon hearing his cries, other inmates of the house, who were present in the nearby fields, arrived at the place of occurrence. The prosecution further alleged that, at about 14:30 hours, the complainant heard the sound of firing emanating from the parental home of his sister-inlaw, Mst. Gul Badan. Upon inquiry, he came to know that the appellant had proceeded to the house of his in-laws and shot dead his wife, Mst. Gul Badan, in the presence of eyewitnesses Mst. Sawab Jan, mother of the deceased (abandoned PW), and Muhammad Rahman. The earlier occurrence, involving the murder of Mst. Rabia Bibi, was allegedly witnessed by the complainant himself. The motive behind the commission of the offences was stated to be strained domestic relations between the parties. On the basis of the complainant’s report, a written complaint (Murasila), Ex. PA/1, was prepared, which culminated in the registration of the instant FIR, Ex. PA, at the police station concerned against the appellant for the alleged murder of his Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din stepmother and wife, albeit in two separate incidents.

4. In criminal cases, the mens rea, or intention of the accused, assumes considerable importance, alongside the nature and gravity of the offence. In the case in hand, the appellant has been charged not only with the murder of his wife, Mst. Gul Badan, within the premises of her parental home, but also with the murder of his stepmother, Mst. Rabia Bibi, within the confines of the parties’ joint residential house. Although the two occurrences took place at separate locations, however, the prosecution asserts that each was witnessed by the most natural witnesses, i.e. the inmates present in the respective residential houses. It further transpires from the record that seven crime empties of .30-bore ammunition were recovered by the police from the first place of occurrence, i.e., the joint residential house where Mst. Rabia Bibi was allegedly murdered. This recovery, when considered in conjunction with the prosecution version, lends prima facie support to the allegation of repeated firing. According to the initial report of the Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din complainant, after sustaining the initial firearm injury, the deceased/mother took refuge in the bathroom; however, the appellant allegedly pursued her there and fired further shots at her vital parts, resulting in her death. Similarly, four crime empties of .30-bore ammunition were recovered from the second place of occurrence. These recoveries, read alongside the other evidence on record, are relevant to the prosecution's allegation that the appellant proceeded from one place of occurrence to the other, armed with a .30-bore pistol, and allegedly committed the second murder at the parental home of his wife, who had been residing there owing to strained matrimonial relations. The medical evidence relating to both deceased women also assumes relevance, as the medical officer reportedly observed multiple firearm injuries on vital parts of their bodies. To the extent that the nature and location of these injuries are consistent with the ocular account and the other incriminating circumstances, such medical evidence lends corroboration to the prosecution version. The repeated firing alleged at the two separate crime scenes, the recoveries of Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din crime empties, and the nature of the injuries sustained by both deceased women are, therefore, circumstances to be assessed collectively in determining the appellant's intention and his alleged culpability for the double murder.

5. To substantiate its case, the prosecution has primarily relied upon the ocular account furnished by two witnesses, whose statements were recorded as PW-13 and PW-14, respectively, in relation to the first occurrence involving the murder of Mst. Rabia Bibi. As regards the second occurrence, pertaining to the murder of Mst. Gul Badan, the prosecution case is supported by the eyewitness account of Muhammad Rehman (PW- 12), besides the medical evidence relating to both deceased women.

6. To substantiate the charge, the complainant, Aman Ullah, real son of deceased Mst. Rabia Bibi, appeared as PW-13. Being the stepbrother of the appellant and an inmate of the same joint residential house, which was the scene of the first occurrence, his presence therein, in the company of his mother, at the relevant time was Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din natural and plausible. In his examination-in-chief, he categorically deposed that the appellant, armed with a .30-bore pistol, arrived at their residential room and opened fire upon his mother, Mst. Rabia Bibi. Having sustained firearm injuries, she attempted to save herself by taking refuge in the bathroom; however, the appellant pursued her and again resorted to firing, causing further injuries to her vital parts. The witness further stated that, after an interval of approximately 20 to 30 minutes, he learnt that the appellant had also murdered his wife, Mst. Gul Badan, at her parental home. The complainant’s presence at the first place of occurrence does not appear to be unnatural or contrived, as he was residing in the same joint household with the appellant and other married brothers. During crossexamination, he specifically stated that he and his five married brothers were living in the said house. Although his presence at the scene was subjected to cross-examination, nothing material could be elicited to discredit his account regarding his presence inside his own residence at the relevant time or his witnessing of the fatal assault upon his mother. His Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din testimony, therefore, derives assurance from the natural circumstances in which he was present and his consistent account of the material features of the occurrence. The fact that PW-13 was closely related to both the deceased and the appellant does not, by itself, render his testimony suspect. Rather, his relationship with the deceased, coupled with his natural presence at the scene, provides a plausible explanation for his witnessing the occurrence. Equally, the mere fact that the appellant was his stepbrother does not establish that the witness had any reason to falsely implicate him in such a grave offence. His testimony must, therefore, be assessed on its intrinsic worth and consistency with the remaining evidence, rather than discarded merely on account of his relationship with the parties. Subject to such overall assessment, the evidence of PW-13 provides direct ocular account of the first occurrence involving the murder of Mst. Rabia Bibi. Likewise, PW-14, the real daughter of the appellant and deceased Mst. Gul Badan, appeared before the Court and furnished an account of the first occurrence. Being a daughter of the appellant and a member of Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din the household, her presence at the place of occurrence was quite natural. She specifically deposed that her father, Fazal Rehman, armed with a pistol, came out of his room and committed the murder of her grandmother, Mst. Rabia Bibi. Her testimony, therefore, provides another direct account of the first occurrence. Its evidentiary worth, like that of any other witness, is to be assessed in the light of its consistency on material particulars and its compatibility with the remaining evidence on record. Her close relationship with the appellant does not, by itself, furnish a sufficient ground to discard her testimony, particularly when her presence in the family home is readily explicable. As regards the second occurrence, Muhammad Rehman appeared as PW-12 and furnished an eyewitness account of the murder of Mst. Gul Badan at her parental home. He deposed that, on the fateful day, he had gone to the house of his paternal aunt, Mst. Sawab Jan, where the deceased was also present. According to him, he was on the rooftop of the house along with the appellant, who asked his wife to come downstairs. Upon her arrival at the lower portion of the house, Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din the appellant took a pistol out of a shopper and opened fire upon her. As a result of the firing, Mst. Gul Badan sustained multiple firearm injuries and died at the spot. The witness thus attributed a specific and direct role to the appellant in the second occurrence.

7. Careful appraisal of the depositions of the prosecution’s star witnesses reveals that they have narrated the mode and manner of both occurrences, attributing specific and distinct roles of firing to the appellant. They have also furnished details regarding the alleged motive, stated to be strained domestic relations between the parties, and identified the weapon of offence as a pistol, allegedly used by the appellant in the commission of the crimes. Their account further suggests that the complainant-party, including both deceased women, had no prior knowledge of the appellant’s arrival at the respective places of occurrence and was unprepared for the sudden armed assault, which, according to the prosecution, left them with little opportunity to avert the fatal consequences. A perusal of the cross-examination of these Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din eyewitnesses indicates that the material particulars concerning the mode and manner of both occurrences, the respective places of occurrence and the presence of the witnesses and the deceased at the relevant times, were put to them and remained substantially intact. No material or dishonest improvement is apparent in their statements, nor does their account, on the basis of the material brought on record, appear inherently unnatural or concocted. Their testimony has, therefore, withstood the searching cross-examination conducted by the learned defence counsel without any material contradiction or infirmity being elicited to discredit their account. In case titled “Aurangzeb v/s State”, the Hon’ble apex Court rendered reasons about presence of the eyewitnesses on the spot qua their natural narrations of the occurrence in terms of specific role of nominated accused [ ]. Same rational was also earlier followed by the Hon’ble apex Court in Muhammad Waris’s case by holding that “sufficient explanation has been offered by the “Aurangzeb v/s State” reported as 2020 SCMR 612. Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din eyewitness about their presence at the venue of crime and witnessing of the subject occurrence” [ ].

8. Learned counsel for the appellant has vehemently contended that the prosecution withheld the most material and natural eyewitness of the second occurrence, namely Mst. Sawab Jan, the mother of deceased Mst. Gul Badan. According to learned counsel, an adverse inference under Article 129(g) of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, is liable to be drawn against the prosecution, as the non-production of the said witness gives rise to the presumption that, had she been examined, her testimony would have been unfavourable to the prosecution case. The contention, however, does not find favour with this Court. The record reveals that another alleged eyewitness of the occurrence, namely Muhammad Rehman, was examined by the prosecution as PW-12, with regard to second occurrence. Thus, the prosecution case is not founded solely upon the testimony of the withheld witness; rather, the prosecution has relied upon the ocular account furnished by PW-12, the evidentiary “Muhammad Waris v/s The State” reported as 2008 SCMR 784. Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din worth of which is to be assessed in the light of the entire material available on record. Furthermore, the prosecution has furnished an explanation for the non-examination of Mst. Sawab Jan, asserting that, owing to her advanced age and loss of hearing, she could not be examined before the Court. In these circumstances, the mere non-production of the said witness does not, by itself, render the prosecution case fatal or necessarily attract an adverse inference under Article 129(g) of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984. The effect of her non-examination must be determined in the context of the explanation furnished by the prosecution and the quality of the evidence otherwise available on record.
Accordingly, the objection raised by learned counsel cannot be accepted merely on the ground that the said witness was not examined.

9. Although certain discrepancies are discernible in the depositions of the prosecution witnesses with regard to the arrival of the police party at the hospital, the omission to name other persons allegedly present at the respective crime scenes besides the eyewitnesses, and the inter-se Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din distance between the places of occurrence and the police station concerned, however, yet such variances pertain to collateral particulars rather than the substratum of the prosecution case. It is pertinent to observe that the witnesses entered the witness-box after a lapse of more than nine months from the occurrence of the tragic incidents. In such circumstances, some divergence in recollection regarding peripheral details is not uncommon and cannot, by itself, furnish a legitimate basis for discarding otherwise consistent ocular testimony. The law does not require a witness to reproduce an occurrence with mathematical exactitude or photographic precision after the passage of time. So long as the discrepancies do not strike at the root of the prosecution case or materially impair the credibility of the witnesses on the essential features of the occurrence, the same are liable to be treated as inconsequential and do not undermine the evidentiary worth of their testimony. Reference can be made to the case of “Khadim Hussain v/s State”, wherein the aforesaid rational of law has explicitly been explained qua creeping of minor Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din contradiction with passage of time [ ]. Reliance can also be placed on the case of “Muhammad Ilyas v/s State” whereby it was held by the Hon’ble apex Court that “contradictions which are not grave in nature can be ignored safely, as minor contradictions creep in with passage of time” [ ].

10. Learned counsel for the appellant has further questioned the credibility of the prosecution witnesses on the premise that all three eyewitnesses were closely related to the deceased women. The objection, however, is devoid of legal force, as consanguinity or close familial association, per se, does not constitute a disqualification rendering a witness incompetent or his testimony unworthy of credence. The Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, in Abdur Rauf v. State and another (2003 SCMR 522), has enunciated the principle “that mere relationship with the deceased is no legal justification for discarding or discrediting the testimony of an eyewitness unless the witness is established to be partisan or interested in the outcome of the prosecution. The touchstone for evaluating ocular testimony is its intrinsic worth, inherent consistency “Khadim Hussain v/s State” reported as PLD 2010 Supreme Court 669. “Muhammad Ilyas v/s State” reported as 2011 SCMR 460. Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din and compatibility with the surrounding circumstances, rather than the mere relationship of the deponent with the deceased. It would be contrary to the settled canons of appreciation of evidence to presume that a related witness is inherently prone to falsehood or that an independent witness is, by virtue of his independence alone, necessarily truthful. The credibility of a witness is to be tested on the touchstone of the quality of his deposition, its intrinsic plausibility and its consonance with the other evidence on record. Where circumstances establish that a witness is actuated by a design to procure the conviction of an innocent person, the Court may look for independent corroboration to dispel the resultant doubt”. In the case in hand, however, the record does not disclose any antecedent blood feud or deep-seated hostility between the parties, apart from the strained domestic relations cited by the prosecution as the motive for the occurrences. No material circumstance has been brought to the fore suggesting that the eyewitnesses were animated by any extraneous consideration or had an ulterior design to falsely implicate the appellant. Likewise, same rational of law was earlier expounded by the Hon’ble apex Court in Amal Sherin’s case by holding that “mere relationship Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din of a witness with deceased would not discredit his/her testimony” [ ]. Refence can also be made to case titled “Khalid v/s State” [ ]. Consequently, the objection founded solely upon the relationship of the eyewitnesses with the deceased women is unsustainable. Their testimony must be weighed on its own merits, in conjunction with the attendant circumstances and the corroborative material available on record, without either attaching undue weight to their relationship or treating it as a ground for automatic rejection.

A perusal of the postmortem reports pertaining to both deceased women reveals that they sustained firearm injuries on vital parts of their bodies during the respective occurrences. The medical evidence is consonant with the ocular account furnished by the three prosecution witnesses and lends corroboration thereto regarding the nature, location and seat of the injuries, as well as the use of a firearm. The medical findings, therefore, lend assurance to the prosecution version and disclose no material inconsistency with the ocular account concerning the manner in which the fatal injuries were allegedly inflicted. Considered in conjunction with the ocular testimony and the other incriminating circumstances brought on record, the medical evidence lends support to the prosecution case. Accordingly, the learned trial Court, having assessed the medical evidence alongside the remaining material on record, was justified in relying upon the same while determining the appellant’s culpability and awarding him the capital punishment for the murder of both deceased women.

Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din 12. The circumstantial evidence also lends support to the prosecution case. During investigation, seven crime empties of .30-bore were recovered from the first place of occurrence, i.e. the residential room situated in the joint house of the parties, vide recovery memo Ex. PW-5/4. Likewise, four crime empties of the same bore were recovered from the second place of occurrence, i.e. the parental house of deceased Mst. Gul Badan, vide recovery memo Ex. PW-6/2. Blood-stained earth was also allegedly secured from both places of occurrence, along with the blood-stained garments of the deceased women. In addition, a .30-bore pistol was recovered at the pointation of the appellant, vide recovery memo Ex. PW-7/4. However, the FSL report, Ex. PK, does not support the prosecution claim regarding the forensic linkage of the recovered weapon with the crime empties, as all eleven empties recovered from the two separate places of occurrence were found not to have been fired from pistol No. 636, allegedly recovered at the instance of the appellant. This circumstance, therefore, deprives the alleged weapon recovery of its corroborative Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din value. Nevertheless, the evidentiary effect of the negative FSL report must be assessed in the context of the entire prosecution case, particularly the ocular account concerning each occurrence, rather than in isolation. Learned counsel for the appellant has argued that the negative FSL report constitutes a mitigating circumstance warranting the reduction of the capital punishment to imprisonment for life. In this regard, it is pertinent to observe that, following the tragic occurrences resulting in the deaths of his stepmother and wife, the appellant allegedly left the locality and remained unavailable until his arrest on 11.10.2024, i.e. four days after the occurrences, pursuant to prior spy information, as reflected in arrest memo Ex. PW-15/16. He neither offered any explanation for his alleged absence in his statement recorded U/S 342, Cr.P.C., nor brought forward any defence plea to account for his conduct. His failure to attend the funeral or other customary proceedings relating to the deceased women, particularly his own wife, may also be considered in the overall assessment of the circumstances, though such conduct, standing alone, cannot establish guilt or Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din substitute for proof of the charge. The decisive question, therefore, is whether the prosecution evidence, independently of the inconclusive weapon recovery, establishes the appellant’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt and, separately, whether the negative forensic result has any bearing on the appropriate sentence. If the ocular account is found reliable and confidence-inspiring, the negative FSL report does not, by itself, discredit that evidence, more particularly in view of the immediate conduct and demeanor of the appellant, soon after the tragic murders of both the deceased.

13. It is a settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that the evidentiary significance of a negative Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) report, particularly regarding the non-matching of crime empties with the recovered firearm, has to be assessed in the light of the attending circumstances of each case. Where an accused is apprehended at the place of occurrence or immediately thereafter from its vicinity, and a weapon is recovered from his possession, the non-matching of the crime empties with the recovered firearm may assume considerable Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din significance and, depending upon the other evidence available on record, may seriously impair the prosecution case. Conversely, where the accused succeeds in fleeing from the scene of occurrence and is arrested after a considerable lapse of time, the evidentiary effect of such non-matching has to be examined from a different perspective. In the latter eventuality, the possibility that the accused might have replaced or changed the weapon of offence during the intervening period cannot be altogether ruled out. Having regard to the prevailing circumstances, the possibility of deliberate replacement of the firearm, with a view to avoiding its subsequent forensic identification with the crime empties, may also be considered, though such possibility must be assessed in the context of the evidence available on record. Thus, mere nonmatching of the recovered firearm with the crime empties, in a case involving delayed arrest of the accused, would not, by itself, necessarily demolish the prosecution case. Accordingly, where the ocular account is confidence-inspiring and consistent on material particulars, the witnesses have satisfactorily Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din established the identity and individual roles of the accused, no material inconsistency exists between the ocular and medical evidence, and the prosecution version receives assurance from other independent circumstances, the negative FSL report would not, in isolation, be sufficient to discard the otherwise reliable ocular account. It is to be borne in mind that an FSL report constitutes expert opinion and is required to be appreciated in conjunction with the entire body of evidence; it cannot be treated as conclusive in isolation or accorded overriding effect so as to displace credible, trustworthy and confidence-inspiring direct evidence. Reference can be made to the judgment of august Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of “Noor Muhammad v. State & another”, wherein it was held that the plea raised by the accused was that according to the opinion of Ballistics Expert, crime empties recovered from the place of incident were fired from seven different weapons. Opinion of Ballistics Expert was not sacrosanct and possibility of error in opining that the empties/bullets secured from the scene of incident were fired from seven different fire-arms could not Nawabwab (D.B.) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Dr. Khurshid Iqbal Hon’ble Mr. Justice Salah-ud-Din be ruled out. No hard and fast rule could be laid down as regards the weight to be given to an Expert's report. Where case otherwise was proved against accused by reliable, truthful and confidenceinspiring evidence, the report of Expert would lose its value. Supreme Court discarded the opinion of Ballistics Expert to the extent of use of seven different weapons” [ ].

14. Prosecution has proved its case against the appellant beyond shadow of doubt through trustworthy, confidence inspiring, corroboratory and circumstantial evidence, which have properly been appreciated by the learned trial Court, hence, the conviction of appellant for the murder of his own wife namely Mst. Gul Badan and stepmother Mst. Rabia Bibi, is not open to any exception.

15. In view of what has been discussed above, the instant criminal appeal being bereft of any merits stands dismissed and the impugned conviction and sentence of the appellant recorded by learned trial Court through impugned judgment dated 16.9.2025, is upheld and maintained.
